title: Αἴας ἐπὶ τὰ ἴκρια
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Achaeans, driven back from the foremost ships, stay all together out of shame and fear, and Nestor begs each man to stand for the sake of his family. Athena lifts the mist from their eyes and they see Hector and his companions. Ajax will not stand with the others; he strides along the decks of the ships with a huge ship-fighting spear, like a rider leaping from horse to horse, and shouts to the Danaans to defend the ships. Hector, thrust on from behind by Zeus, rushes at a ship like an eagle at river birds, and the fighting round the ship that carried Protesilaus is hand to hand, with axes, swords and spears. Hector takes hold of its stern and bids the Trojans bring fire, since Zeus has given them the day. Ajax, hard pressed by missiles, draws back to the seven-foot footstool, and from there keeps off every Trojan who brings fire. He tells the Danaans that they have no wall or city behind them and must save themselves with their hands, and he wounds twelve men in front of the ships.

sentences.t:
εἰσωποὶ δ’ ἐγένοντο νεῶν, περὶ δ’ ἔσχεθον ἄκραι
νῆες ὅσαι πρῶται εἰρύατο· τοὶ δ’ ἐπέχυντο.
sentences.tr:
eisōpoi d’ egenonto neōn, peri d’ eschethon akrai
nēes hosai prōtai eiryato· toi d’ epechynto.
sentences.l:
In view of the ships they came to be, and around held the outermost
ships, as many as had been drawn up first; and they poured on.
sentences.i: They came to stand right before the ships, and the outermost ships, all that had been drawn up first, held them round about; and the Trojans poured on.
sentences.n: Nobody is named as the subject of the first verb; they are the Achaeans of the last unit of the previous part, who were afraid of Hector, set against the Trojans (τοί) at the end of this sentence; the Argives of the next sentence are the same army under another name. εἰσωποί ‘in sight of, facing’ takes the genitive νεῶν. In περὶ δ’ ἔσχεθον the preverb περί stands apart from its verb (tmesis), and ἔσχεθον is an epic aorist of ἔχω. The subject is ἄκραι νῆες ‘the outermost ships’, and no object is given: ‘them’, the Achaeans, is understood, and the exact sense (‘held them in a ring’, ‘closed round them’) is not certain; the English says ‘held them round about’. εἰρύατο is the epic third plural of ἐρύω ‘draw’ in the passive, ‘had been drawn up’ on the shore. τοὶ δ’ ἐπέχυντο is ‘and they poured on’, an aorist middle of ἐπιχέω.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δὲ νεῶν μὲν ἐχώρησαν καὶ ἀνάγκῃ
τῶν πρωτέων, αὐτοῦ δὲ παρὰ κλισίῃσιν ἔμειναν
ἁθρόοι, οὐδὲ κέδασθεν ἀνὰ στρατόν·
sentences.tr:
Argeioi de neōn men echōrēsan kai anankēi
tōn prōteōn, autou de para klisiēisin emeinan
hathrooi, oude kedasthen ana straton·
sentences.i: Of necessity the Argives gave way from the ships, from the foremost ones, but they stayed there beside the huts, all together, and did not scatter through the army;
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is the army under its third name, kept as the poet chose it. νεῶν is a genitive of separation after ἐχώρησαν ‘gave way, withdrew’, and τῶν πρωτέων (= τῶν πρώτων) says which ships: ‘the foremost ones’. ἀνάγκῃ is a dative, ‘by necessity’. μὲν is answered by δέ in αὐτοῦ δὲ … ἔμειναν ‘but on the spot … they stayed’. κλισίῃσιν is the epic dative plural of κλισίη ‘hut’. ἁθρόοι is the edition’s spelling of ἀθρόοι ‘all together’. κέδασθεν is an aorist passive of κεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, with no augment.

sentences.t:
ἴσχε γὰρ αἰδὼς
καὶ δέος·
sentences.tr:
ische gar aidōs
kai deos·
sentences.l:
for restrained them shame
and fear;
sentences.i: for shame and fear held them back;
sentences.n: ἴσχε is the imperfect of ἴσχω ‘hold back’, and no object is given: ‘it held them back’. The two subjects are αἰδώς ‘shame’, the regard for what others will think (the same word as αἰδῶ in Nestor’s speech below), and δέος ‘fear’. The line breaks off at a raised stop, and the next sentence adds what they were doing while held there.

sentences.t: ἀζηχὲς γὰρ ὁμόκλεον ἀλλήλοισι.
sentences.tr: azēches gar homokleon allēloisi.
sentences.l: for incessantly they shouted to one another.
sentences.i: for they shouted to one another incessantly.
sentences.n: ἀζηχές is an adverb, ‘incessantly’. ὁμόκλεον is the imperfect of ὁμοκλέω ‘shout’, uncontracted; the verb can carry a sense of rebuke or threat, but here it is simply what they kept calling out ἀλλήλοισι ‘to one another’. This is a second γάρ clause, adding to the first.

sentences.t:
Νέστωρ αὖτε μάλιστα Γερήνιος οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν
λίσσεθ’ ὑπὲρ τοκέων γουνούμενος ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr:
Nestōr aute malista Gerēnios ouros Achaiōn
lisseth’ hyper tokeōn gounoumenos andra hekaston·
sentences.l:
And Nestor, in turn, most of all, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans,
begged, for the sake of their parents, beseeching each man:
sentences.i: And Nestor, in his turn, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans, begged each man most of all, entreating him for his parents’ sake:
sentences.n: The first line has the same words as 15.370. Γερήνιος οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν is the stock phrase ‘the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans’, translated every time; why Nestor is called Gerenian is not explained here. αὖτε ‘in turn’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’ may go with Nestor (‘above all’) or with the begging; the Greek does not settle it, and the English follows iliad-094, where the same words stand. λίσσεθ’ is λίσσετο, the imperfect of λίσσομαι ‘beg’. ὑπὲρ τοκέων is ‘for the sake of parents’: the appeal to what each man holds dear, which the speech then spells out. γουνούμενος is from γουνόομαι ‘beseech’, a verb built on γόνυ ‘knee’ (‘beseeching’ in the literal layer, ‘entreating’ in the other), the knee-clasping of a suppliant, though here only the word is used. The raised stop is English’s colon, and Nestor’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἀνέρες ἔστε καὶ αἰδῶ θέσθ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων, ἐπὶ δὲ μνήσασθε ἕκαστος
παίδων ἠδ’ ἀλόχων καὶ κτήσιος ἠδὲ τοκήων,
ἠμὲν ὅτεῳ ζώουσι καὶ ᾧ κατατεθνήκασι·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi aneres este kai aidō thesth’ eni thymōi
allōn anthrōpōn, epi de mnēsasthe hekastos
paidōn ēd’ alochōn kai ktēsios ēde tokēōn,
ēmen hoteōi zōousi kai hōi katatethnēkasi·
sentences.l:
“Friends, be men, and put shame in your heart
of other men, and be mindful, each of you,
of children and of wives and of possessions and of parents,
both for whom they live and for whom they have died;
sentences.i: “Friends, be men, and put shame in your hearts before other men, and each of you remember your children and wives and property and parents, whether they are living for you or have died;
sentences.n: Nestor speaks. The first line is the one Ajax used at 15.561, there with a comma after ἔστε. ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ, and ἔστε the imperative ‘be’. αἰδῶ θέσθ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ is ‘put shame in your heart’, and ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων is a genitive of the people before whom one feels it. ἐπὶ … μνήσασθε is tmesis for ἐπιμνήσασθε ‘be mindful of’, which takes the genitives παίδων, ἀλόχων, κτήσιος (epic genitive of κτῆσις ‘property’) and τοκήων; ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is in apposition to the ‘you’. ἠμὲν … καί is ‘both … and’, with καί standing where ἠδέ is more usual. ὅτεῳ is the epic dative of ὅστις, and ᾧ is a relative dative: ‘for whom they live’ and ‘for whom they have died’, a dative of the person concerned. ζώουσι is the uncontracted ζῶσι, and κατατεθνήκασι the perfect of καταθνῄσκω ‘have died’.

sentences.t:
τῶν ὕπερ ἐνθάδ’ ἐγὼ γουνάζομαι οὐ παρεόντων
ἑστάμεναι κρατερῶς, μὴ δὲ τρωπᾶσθε φόβον δέ.
sentences.tr:
tōn hyper enthad’ egō gounazomai ou pareontōn
hestamenai kraterōs, mē de trōpasthe phobon de.
sentences.l:
on behalf of them, here, I entreat you, who are not present,
to stand strongly, and turn not toward flight.”
sentences.i: For their sake, though they are not present, I entreat you here to stand your ground strongly, and do not turn to flight.”
sentences.n: τῶν ὕπερ is ὑπὲρ τῶν with the preposition after its noun, ‘for the sake of those’, picking up the family just listed; οὐ παρεόντων ‘who are not present’ agrees with τῶν. γουνάζομαι ‘I entreat’ is from the same root as γουνούμενος above. ἑστάμεναι is a perfect infinitive in -μεναι of ἵστημι (the perfect means ‘be standing’), giving what he begs: ‘to stand’. κρατερῶς ‘strongly’. μὴ δέ is μηδέ ‘and not’ written as two words, and τρωπᾶσθε is the present imperative of τρωπάομαι, a by-form of τρέπομαι ‘turn’. φόβον δέ is the accusative with the suffix -δε, ‘toward flight’; φόβος in battle is the running that fear drives. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: The same line stands at 5.470. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is an aorist participle. ὄτρυνε is a past tense without the augment, from ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. μένος ‘might’ and θυμός ‘heart’ are the fighting force and the spirit, and ἑκάστου is ‘of each man’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν νέφος ἀχλύος ὦσεν Ἀθήνη
θεσπέσιον·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ ap’ ophthalmōn nephos achlyos ōsen Athēnē
thespesion·
sentences.l:
And from their eyes the cloud of mist Athena thrust away,
a wondrous one;
sentences.i: And Athena thrust the wondrous cloud of mist away from their eyes;
sentences.n: τοῖσι is a dative of interest, ‘for them’, the Achaeans. νέφος ἀχλύος is ‘a cloud of mist’, with ἀχλύος a genitive saying what the cloud is made of; ὦσεν is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’. θεσπέσιον ‘wondrous’ is set at the start of the next line and agrees with νέφος; it is the house ‘wondrous’. The raised stop ends the clause, and the next gives the result.

sentences.t:
μάλα δέ σφι φόως γένετ’ ἀμφοτέρωθεν
ἠμὲν πρὸς νηῶν καὶ ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
mala de sphi phoōs genet’ amphoterōthen
ēmen pros nēōn kai homoiïou polemoio.
sentences.l:
and greatly to them light came on both sides,
both on the side of the ships and of the war common to all.
sentences.i: and a great light came to them on both sides, on the side of the ships and on the side of the war that is common to all.
sentences.n: σφι is the epic dative ‘to them’. μάλα ‘greatly’ goes with φόως (= φάος) ‘light’, and γένετο is an aorist with no augment (= ἐγένετο). ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘on both sides’. ἠμὲν … καί ‘both … and’, and πρὸς νηῶν is ‘on the side of the ships’ (πρός with the genitive). ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο is ‘war common to all’, the Iliad’s rendering of ὁμοίϊος, which is built on ὅμοιος ‘like, the same’; its exact sense (‘common to both sides’, ‘equal’) is not certain; the English keeps one reading.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δὲ φράσσαντο βοὴν ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἑταίρους,
ἠμὲν ὅσοι μετόπισθεν ἀφέστασαν οὐδὲ μάχοντο,
ἠδ’ ὅσσοι παρὰ νηυσὶ μάχην ἐμάχοντο θοῇσιν.
sentences.tr:
Hektora de phrassanto boēn agathon kai hetairous,
ēmen hosoi metopisthen aphestasan oude machonto,
ēd’ hossoi para nēusi machēn emachonto thoēisin.
sentences.l:
And Hector they perceived, good at the war-cry, and his companions,
both as many as stood apart behind and were not fighting,
and as many as beside the swift ships fought the fight.
sentences.i: They saw Hector, good at the war-cry, and his companions, both those who stood apart behind and were not fighting, and those who were fighting beside the swift ships.
sentences.n: The subject, carried over from τοῖσι, is the Achaeans, who can now see. φράσσαντο is the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘notice, perceive’. Ἕκτορα … βοὴν ἀγαθόν is the stock phrase ‘Hector, good at the war-cry’ (βοήν is an accusative of respect), translated every time. ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’. μετόπισθεν ‘behind’. ἀφέστασαν is the pluperfect of ἀφίστημι, ‘stood apart’; μάχοντο is the imperfect of μάχομαι with no augment, and μάχην ἐμάχοντο ‘fought the fight’ has the cognate accusative.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ Αἴαντι μεγαλήτορι ἥνδανε θυμῷ
ἑστάμεν ἔνθά περ ἄλλοι ἀφέστασαν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ et’ Aianti megalētori hēndane thymōi
hestamen entha per alloi aphestasan huies Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
And no longer to Ajax, great-spirited, was it pleasing in his heart
to stand where the other sons of the Achaeans stood apart;
sentences.i: And no longer did it please great-spirited Ajax in his heart to stand just where the other sons of the Achaeans stood apart;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ is ‘and then no longer’. ἥνδανε is the imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘be pleasing’, with the person in the dative (Αἴαντι) and θυμῷ ‘in his heart’ a dative of respect; what pleased is the infinitive ἑστάμεν (= ἑστάμεναι) ‘to stand’. μεγαλήτωρ is the stock epithet ‘great-spirited’. ἔνθά περ is ‘just where’, and ἀφέστασαν is ‘stood apart’ again, as at 672.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε νηῶν ἴκρι’ ἐπῴχετο μακρὰ βιβάσθων,
νώμα δὲ ξυστὸν μέγα ναύμαχον ἐν παλάμῃσι
κολλητὸν βλήτροισι δυωκαιεικοσίπηχυ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho ge nēōn ikri’ epōicheto makra bibasthōn,
nōma de xyston mega naumachon en palamēisi
kollēton blētroisi dyōkaieikosipēchy.
sentences.l:
but he went along the decks of the ships, taking long strides,
and wielded a great ship-fighting polished spear in his hands,
glued with clamps, twenty-two cubits long.
sentences.i: But he went along the decks of the ships, taking long strides, and wielded in his hands a great polished spear made for fighting at sea, glued together with clamps and twenty-two cubits long.
sentences.n: ἴκρια is the decking of a ship, a plural word; the planks along which Ajax runs from ship to ship, though what exactly the fitting was is not known. ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι ‘go along’, and μακρὰ βιβάσθων is ‘striding long’, a present participle of βιβάσθω, a lengthened form of the verb for walking, with μακρά used as an adverb. ξυστόν is the house ‘polished spear’, here a monstrous one; ναύμαχον ‘ship-fighting’ is the adjective used of spears at 15.389; νώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘wield’. κολλητόν ‘glued together’ (the house ‘glued’ of κολλήεις) goes with βλήτροισι, the dative of βλῆτρον, a rare word whose sense is uncertain (a ring, band or clamp holding the pieces); the English says ‘clamps’. δυωκαιεικοσίπηχυ ‘twenty-two cubits long’ is one word, from δύο καὶ εἴκοσι and πῆχυς ‘cubit’, a forearm’s length, so something like ten metres.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ ἵπποισι κελητίζειν ἐῢ εἰδώς,
ὅς τ’ ἐπεὶ ἐκ πολέων πίσυρας συναείρεται ἵππους,
σεύας ἐκ πεδίοιο μέγα προτὶ ἄστυ δίηται
λαοφόρον καθ’ ὁδόν·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ anēr hippoisi kelētizein eÿ eidōs,
hos t’ epei ek poleōn pisyras synaeiretai hippous,
seuas ek pedioio mega proti asty diētai
laophoron kath’ hodon·
sentences.l:
And as when a man, knowing well how to ride horses,
who, when out of many he has yoked together four horses,
and set them moving from the plain, drives hard toward the city
along the people-bearing road;
sentences.i: And as when a man who knows well how to ride horses has harnessed four out of many together, and, urging them from the plain, drives them hard toward the city along the road that carries the people;
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ‘and as when’. ἵπποισι κελητίζειν ἐῢ εἰδώς is ‘knowing well how to ride horses’: κελητίζειν is from κέλης ‘riding-horse’, riding on a horse’s back as opposed to driving a chariot. πίσυρας is the epic ‘four’ (= τέσσαρας). συναείρεται is the middle of συναείρω ‘yoke together’, and ἐκ πολέων ‘out of many’ means he picks four from a larger number. σεύας is the aorist participle of σεύω ‘set moving’, and δίηται is a subjunctive of δίεμαι ‘drive on, speed’ (the usual parse), in a general simile. μέγα goes with it, ‘hard’. λαοφόρον is ‘people-bearing’, a road that carries traffic, a much-used road.

sentences.t:
πολέες τέ ἑ θηήσαντο
ἀνέρες ἠδὲ γυναῖκες·
sentences.tr:
polees te he thēēsanto
aneres ēde gynaikes·
sentences.l:
and many have gazed at him in wonder,
men and women;
sentences.i: and many men and women gaze at him in wonder;
sentences.n: πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί ‘many’, and ἑ is ‘him’. θηήσαντο is the aorist of θηέομαι ‘gaze at in wonder’, used as in similes for what regularly happens, so English says ‘gaze’. ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔμπεδον ἀσφαλὲς αἰεὶ
θρῴσκων ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλον ἀμείβεται, οἳ δὲ πέτονται·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ empedon asphales aiei
thrōiskōn allot’ ep’ allon ameibetai, hoi de petontai·
sentences.l:
while he steadily, securely, ever,
leaping, from one to another changes, and they fly;
sentences.i: while he, always steady and secure, leaps now to one horse, now to another, and they fly along;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘but he’, the rider. ἔμπεδον ἀσφαλές ‘steadily, securely’ are neuter adjectives used as adverbs, and αἰεί ‘ever’ goes with them. θρῴσκων is the present participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλον is ‘now onto one, now onto another’, with ‘horse’ understood. ἀμείβεται is here ‘changes (his place), passes over’, not the ‘answer’ that the verb means in speeches. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the horses, and πέτονται ‘fly’ is the present of πέτομαι.

sentences.t:
ὣς Αἴας ἐπὶ πολλὰ θοάων ἴκρια νηῶν
φοίτα μακρὰ βιβάς, φωνὴ δέ οἱ αἰθέρ’ ἵκανεν,
αἰεὶ δὲ σμερδνὸν βοόων Δαναοῖσι κέλευε
νηυσί τε καὶ κλισίῃσιν ἀμυνέμεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs Aias epi polla thoaōn ikria nēōn
phoita makra bibas, phōnē de hoi aither’ hikanen,
aiei de smerdnon booōn Danaoisi keleue
nēusi te kai klisiēisin amynemen.
sentences.l:
So Ajax over the many decks of the swift ships
went to and fro, taking long strides, and his voice reached the upper air,
and ever terribly shouting he bade the Danaans
to ward off from the ships and the huts.
sentences.i: So Ajax went to and fro over the many decks of the swift ships, taking long strides, and his voice reached the upper air; and ever shouting terribly he bade the Danaans ward off harm from the ships and the huts.
sentences.n: ὣς Αἴας closes the simile. ἐπὶ πολλά … ἴκρια is ‘over many decks’, with ἐπί and the accusative, and θοάων is the epic genitive plural of θοός ‘swift’. φοίτα is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘range to and fro’. μακρὰ βιβάς is ‘striding long’, a participle of the same family as βιβάσθων at 676. αἰθέρ’ is the accusative of αἰθήρ, the bright upper air, and οἱ is ‘his’. σμερδνόν is an adverb, ‘terribly’, and βοόων the uncontracted βοῶν ‘shouting’. κέλευε is the imperfect ‘bade’, with the infinitive ἀμυνέμεν (epic form of ἀμύνειν) and the datives νηυσί … κλισίῃσιν: ‘ward off (harm) from the ships and huts’: ἀμύνω with the dative means ‘ward off danger for’, and no object is given.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν Ἕκτωρ
μίμνεν ἐνὶ Τρώων ὁμάδῳ πύκα θωρηκτάων·
sentences.tr:
oude men Hektōr
mimnen eni Trōōn homadōi pyka thōrēktaōn·
sentences.l:
And Hector, for his part, did not stay
in the uproar of the closely corseleted Trojans;
sentences.i: But Hector, for his part, did not stay in the noisy crowd of the closely corseleted Trojans;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μὲν is ‘nor indeed’, here in effect ‘and Hector, on his side, did not’. μίμνεν is the imperfect of μίμνω ‘stay’, with no augment (compare ἔμιμνε at 727). ὁμάδῳ is the dative of ὅμαδος, the noise a crowd makes, and so the crowd (‘uproar’ in the literal layer, ‘noisy crowd’ in the other). Τρώων … πύκα θωρηκτάων is the stock phrase ‘of the closely corseleted Trojans’, with the epic genitive plural in -άων.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τ’ ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν αἰετὸς αἴθων
ἔθνος ἐφορμᾶται ποταμὸν πάρα βοσκομενάων
χηνῶν ἢ γεράνων ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων,
sentences.tr:
all’ hōs t’ ornithōn peteēnōn aietos aithōn
ethnos ephormatai potamon para boskomenaōn
chēnōn ē geranōn ē kyknōn doulichodeirōn,
sentences.l:
But as an eagle, fire-bright, rushes upon a tribe of winged birds
feeding beside a river,
of geese or of cranes or of long-necked swans,
sentences.i: But as a fire-bright eagle rushes upon a swarm of winged birds feeding beside a river, geese or cranes or long-necked swans,
sentences.n: Another simile, with ὥς τ’ ‘as’. ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ‘of winged birds’ is a genitive going with ἔθνος ‘tribe, swarm’, the object of ἐφορμᾶται ‘rushes upon’. αἴθων is the house ‘fire-bright’; it is a word of colour or flash, and the exact shade is not known. ποταμὸν πάρα is παρὰ ποταμόν with the preposition after its noun, and βοσκομενάων is the epic genitive plural feminine of βοσκόμενος ‘feeding’. The third line is the same as 2.460. δουλιχοδείρων is the epic form of δολιχόδειρος ‘long-necked’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἴθυσε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
ἀντίος ἀΐξας·
sentences.tr:
hōs Hektōr ithyse neos kyanoprōiroio
antios aïxas·
sentences.l:
so Hector made straight for a dark-prowed ship,
rushing against it;
sentences.i: so Hector made straight for a dark-prowed ship, darting at it head-on;
sentences.n: ὣς Ἕκτωρ closes the simile. ἴθυσε is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’, and it takes the genitive νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο ‘a dark-prowed ship’ (the stock adjective, translated every time); the ship is not named yet. ἀντίος is ‘opposite, face to face’, and ἀΐξας the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ Ζεὺς ὦσεν ὄπισθε
χειρὶ μάλα μεγάλῃ, ὄτρυνε δὲ λαὸν ἅμ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
ton de Zeus ōsen opisthe
cheiri mala megalēi, otryne de laon ham’ autōi.
sentences.l:
and him Zeus thrust from behind
with a very great hand, and urged on the people along with him.
sentences.i: and Zeus thrust him on from behind with a very great hand and urged the people on along with him.
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, Hector. ὦσεν ‘thrust’ is the same verb as at 668, where Athena removes the mist. ὄπισθε ‘from behind’. χειρὶ μάλα μεγάλῃ is a dative of means, ‘with a very great hand’. ὄτρυνε has no augment, and λαόν is ‘the people, the host’, with ἅμ’ αὐτῷ ‘along with him’.

sentences.t: αὖτις δὲ δριμεῖα μάχη παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐτύχθη·
sentences.tr: autis de drimeia machē para nēusin etychthē·
sentences.l: And again sharp fighting beside the ships was made;
sentences.i: And again sharp fighting arose beside the ships;
sentences.n: αὖτις ‘again’. δριμεῖα ‘sharp, keen’ agrees with μάχη, which the house keeps as ‘fighting’. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make’, so ‘was made’, i.e. ‘came about’; the English says ‘arose’.

sentences.t:
φαίης κ’ ἀκμῆτας καὶ ἀτειρέας ἀλλήλοισιν
ἄντεσθ’ ἐν πολέμῳ, ὡς ἐσσυμένως ἐμάχοντο.
sentences.tr:
phaiēs k’ akmētas kai ateireas allēloisin
antesth’ en polemōi, hōs essymenōs emachonto.
sentences.l:
you would say, fresh and unwearied, that against one another
they met in war, so eagerly were they fighting.
sentences.i: You would have said that they met one another in the war fresh and unwearied, so eagerly did they fight.
sentences.n: φαίης κ’ is a present optative of φημί with κε, ‘you would say’, a turn to the listener. ἀκμῆτας ‘fresh’ and ἀτειρέας ‘unwearied’ are accusatives going with the unstated subject of the infinitive ἄντεσθ’ (= ἄντεσθαι, from ἄντομαι ‘meet’). ἐσσυμένως is the adverb of ἐσσύμενος ‘eager’; ὡς ‘so’ goes with it, and ἐμάχοντο is ‘fought’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μαρναμένοισιν ὅδ’ ἦν νόος·
sentences.tr: toisi de marnamenoisin hod’ ēn noos·
sentences.l: And to them as they fought this was the mind:
sentences.i: And as they fought, this was the thought in their minds:
sentences.n: τοῖσι … μαρναμένοισιν is a dative, ‘to them as they fought’, and ὅδ’ ἦν νόος is ‘this was the mind’: νόος is the purpose or thought, and ὅδε ‘this’ points forward to the next unit. The raised stop is English’s colon.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι Ἀχαιοὶ
οὐκ ἔφασαν φεύξεσθαι ὑπ’ ἐκ κακοῦ, ἀλλ’ ὀλέεσθαι,
Τρωσὶν δ’ ἔλπετο θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἑκάστου
νῆας ἐνιπρήσειν κτενέειν θ’ ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
ētoi Achaioi
ouk ephasan pheuxesthai hyp’ ek kakou, all’ oleesthai,
Trōsin d’ elpeto thymos eni stēthessin hekastou
nēas eniprēsein kteneein th’ hērōas Achaious.
sentences.l:
Indeed the Achaeans
said they would not escape out from under the evil, but would perish,
while for the Trojans the heart hoped, in the breast of each,
to set the ships on fire and to kill the hero Achaeans.
sentences.i: The Achaeans, for their part, said that they would not escape from the evil but would perish; but in the breast of each Trojan the heart hoped to set the ships on fire and kill the Achaean heroes.
sentences.n: The two sides’ thoughts are set against one another: ἤτοι ‘truly’ marks the first, and δ’ in Τρωσὶν δ’ the second. οὐκ ἔφασαν φεύξεσθαι is ‘said they would not escape’, with the negative on the verb of saying; φεύξεσθαι is the future infinitive of φεύγω, and ὑπ’ ἐκ κακοῦ is ‘out from under the evil’. ὀλέεσθαι is the uncontracted future infinitive of ὄλλυμι, ‘perish’. Τρωσίν is a dative of the persons whose heart it is; ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’, and ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ‘in the breast’ has the epic dative plural. ἐνιπρήσειν is the future infinitive of ἐνιπίμπρημι ‘set on fire’, and κτενέειν the uncontracted future infinitive of κτείνω ‘kill’. ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς is ‘the Achaean heroes’.

sentences.t: οἳ μὲν τὰ φρονέοντες ἐφέστασαν ἀλλήλοισιν·
sentences.tr: hoi men ta phroneontes ephestasan allēloisin·
sentences.l: These, thinking these thoughts, stood against one another;
sentences.i: Thinking such thoughts, they stood facing one another;
sentences.n: οἳ μέν is ‘these’, the two armies, and Ἕκτωρ δέ in the next unit goes back to the single man. τὰ φρονέοντες is ‘thinking these things’, φρονέοντες uncontracted. ἐφέστασαν is the pluperfect of ἐφίστημι, ‘stood against, stood facing’, with ἀλλήλοισιν ‘one another’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ πρυμνῆς νεὸς ἥψατο ποντοπόροιο
καλῆς ὠκυάλου, ἣ Πρωτεσίλαον ἔνεικεν
ἐς Τροίην, οὐδ’ αὖτις ἀπήγαγε πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
Hektōr de prymnēs neos hēpsato pontoporoio
kalēs ōkyalou, hē Prōtesilaon eneiken
es Troiēn, oud’ autis apēgage patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
And Hector laid hold of the stern of a sea-crossing ship,
fair and swift-sailing, which carried Protesilaus
to Troy, and did not bring him back again to his fatherland.
sentences.i: Hector laid hold of the stern of a sea-crossing ship, a fair, swift-sailing one, that had carried Protesilaus to Troy and had not brought him back again to his fatherland.
sentences.n: πρυμνῆς νεός is ‘of the hindmost ship’ in form, since the adjective πρυμνός ‘hindmost’ agrees with νεός; the sense is the ship’s hind end, the stern. ἥψατο is the aorist middle of ἅπτω, which takes the genitive. ποντοπόροιο ‘sea-crossing’ and ὠκυάλου ‘swift-sailing’ (ὠκύς and ἅλς ‘sea’) are stock adjectives, and καλῆς is ‘fair’. ἣ is the relative ‘which’. ἔνεικεν is the aorist of φέρω, ‘carried’, and ἀπήγαγε the aorist of ἀπάγω ‘lead away’, here ‘take back home’. Πρωτεσίλαον is the man whose ship it was; the lines say only that he went to Troy in it and was not taken home again.

sentences.t:
τοῦ περ δὴ περὶ νηὸς Ἀχαιοί τε Τρῶές τε
δῄουν ἀλλήλους αὐτοσχεδόν·
sentences.tr:
tou per dē peri nēos Achaioi te Trōes te
dēioun allēlous autoschedon·
sentences.l:
And around that very ship Achaeans and Trojans
were hacking at one another at close quarters;
sentences.i: And around that very ship Achaeans and Trojans hacked at one another at close quarters;
sentences.n: τοῦ is the demonstrative ‘that’, and περ δή stresses it: ‘that very ship’. δῄουν is the uncontracted imperfect of δηϊόω ‘hack at, cut down’; ‘hacked at’ is the house rendering of this form. ἀλλήλους ‘one another’, and αὐτοσχεδόν ‘at close quarters’ is an adverb.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γε
τόξων ἀϊκὰς ἀμφὶς μένον οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀκόντων,
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara toi ge
toxōn aïkas amphis menon oud’ et’ akontōn,
sentences.l:
nor did they, for their part,
wait apart for the rush of arrows from bows, nor any more of javelins,
sentences.i: And they did not stand apart and wait for the rush of arrows from bows, or any longer for javelins,
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γε is ‘nor then did they’. ἀϊκάς, accusative plural of ἀϊκή, is a rare word for the rush or whizz of a missile, and its exact sense is not certain. τόξων is ‘of bows’, so ‘the rush of bow-shots’. ἀμφίς ‘apart’, and μένον (= ἔμενον, with no augment) ‘waited for’; οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀκόντων ‘nor any more of javelins’ gives a second thing they did not wait for.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἵ γ’ ἐγγύθεν ἱστάμενοι ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες
ὀξέσι δὴ πελέκεσσι καὶ ἀξίνῃσι μάχοντο
καὶ ξίφεσιν μεγάλοισι καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι.
sentences.tr:
all’ hoi g’ engythen histamenoi hena thymon echontes
oxesi dē pelekessi kai axinēisi machonto
kai xiphesin megaloisi kai enchesin amphigyoisi.
sentences.l:
but standing near, with one heart,
they fought with sharp axes and with battle-axes
and with great swords and with double-pointed spears.
sentences.i: but standing close, of one heart, they fought with sharp axes and battle-axes and with great swords and double-pointed spears.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οἵ γ’ is ‘but they’. ἐγγύθεν ἱστάμενοι is ‘standing near’ one another, and ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες ‘having one heart’ is the phrase for acting as one. πελέκεσσι and ἀξίνῃσι are two Greek words for axes; the house table renders each as ‘axe’, so here the second is ‘battle-axes’ to keep them apart, with δή only emphasising. The datives are of instrument, and μάχοντο is an imperfect with no augment. ξίφεσιν μεγάλοισι ‘great swords’; ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι ‘double-pointed spears’ is the stock phrase; the meaning of ἀμφίγυος is not known, and ‘double-pointed’ is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ φάσγανα καλὰ μελάνδετα κωπήεντα
ἄλλα μὲν ἐκ χειρῶν χαμάδις πέσον, ἄλλα δ’ ἀπ’ ὤμων
ἀνδρῶν μαρναμένων·
sentences.tr:
polla de phasgana kala melandeta kōpēenta
alla men ek cheirōn chamadis peson, alla d’ ap’ ōmōn
andrōn marnamenōn·
sentences.i: And many fine swords, dark-bound and hilted, fell to the ground, some from hands and others from the shoulders of men as they fought;
sentences.n: πολλὰ … φάσγανα καλά is ‘many fine swords’. μελάνδετα is a rare compound of μέλας ‘dark’ and δετός ‘bound’; what is bound dark (hilt, sword-strap or scabbard) is not known, and the English says ‘dark-bound’. κωπήεντα is ‘hilted’, from κώπη ‘hilt’. ἄλλα μὲν … ἄλλα δ’ is ‘some … others’. ἐκ χειρῶν ‘out of hands’, ἀπ’ ὤμων ‘from shoulders’, and χαμάδις ‘to the ground’; πέσον is an aorist with no augment. ἀνδρῶν μαρναμένων ‘of men fighting’ goes with both χειρῶν and ὤμων.

sentences.t: ῥέε δ’ αἵματι γαῖα μέλαινα.
sentences.tr: rhee d’ haimati gaia melaina.
sentences.l: and with blood ran the dark earth.
sentences.i: and the dark earth ran with blood.
sentences.n: ῥέε is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’, without the augment (augmented, it would be ἔρρεε). αἵματι is a dative of means, ‘with blood’, and γαῖα μέλαινα is the stock phrase ‘the dark earth’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ πρύμνηθεν ἐπεὶ λάβεν οὐχὶ μεθίει
ἄφλαστον μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων, Τρωσὶν δὲ κέλευεν·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr de prymnēthen epei laben ouchi methiei
aphlaston meta chersin echōn, Trōsin de keleuen·
sentences.l:
But Hector, when he took hold at the stern, did not let go,
holding the stern-ornament in his hands, and bade the Trojans:
sentences.i: But Hector, once he had taken hold at the stern, did not let go; he held the stern-ornament in his hands and bade the Trojans:
sentences.n: λάβεν is the aorist of λαμβάνω with no augment, and πρύμνηθεν is ‘from the stern’, the suffix -θεν marking the place the hold is taken. μεθίει is the imperfect of μεθίημι ‘let go’. ἄφλαστον is a part of a ship’s stern, traditionally taken as an ornamental stern-piece; its exact form is not known, and the English says ‘stern-ornament’. μετὰ χερσίν is ‘in his hands’ (μετά with the dative), and ἔχων ‘holding’. κέλευεν is ‘bade’ with Τρωσίν in the dative, and the raised stop opens Hector’s speech.

sentences.t: οἴσετε πῦρ, ἅμα δ’ αὐτοὶ ἀολλέες ὄρνυτ’ ἀϋτήν·
sentences.tr: oisete pyr, hama d’ autoi aollees ornyt’ aÿtēn·
sentences.l: “Bring fire, and at the same time yourselves, in a close mass, raise the battle-cry;
sentences.i: “Bring fire, and at the same time, in a close mass, raise the battle-cry yourselves;
sentences.n: Hector speaks. οἴσετε is the plural imperative of the aorist of φέρω ‘bring’. ἅμα δ’ αὐτοί is ‘and at the same time yourselves’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ is the house rendering. ὄρνυτ’ is ὄρνυτε, the imperative of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse, raise’, and ἀϋτή is a shout or battle-cry.

sentences.t:
νῦν ἡμῖν πάντων Ζεὺς ἄξιον ἦμαρ ἔδωκε
νῆας ἑλεῖν, αἳ δεῦρο θεῶν ἀέκητι μολοῦσαι
ἡμῖν πήματα πολλὰ θέσαν, κακότητι γερόντων,
sentences.tr:
nyn hēmin pantōn Zeus axion ēmar edōke
nēas helein, hai deuro theōn aekēti molousai
hēmin pēmata polla thesan, kakotēti gerontōn,
sentences.l:
now to us the day worth all Zeus has given
to take the ships, which coming here against the will of the gods
have laid on us many woes, through the baseness of the elders,
sentences.i: now Zeus has given us a day worth everything, to take the ships, which came here against the will of the gods and laid many woes on us, through the baseness of the elders,
sentences.n: ἄξιον ἦμαρ πάντων is ‘a day worth all’: ἄξιος takes a genitive of what it is worth, and πάντων may be ‘all things’ or ‘all (other days)’; the English says ‘worth everything’. νῆας ἑλεῖν is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to take the ships’. αἳ … μολοῦσαι is ‘which having come’ (aorist participle of βλώσκω), and θεῶν ἀέκητι is ‘against the will of the gods’. θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι with no augment, so πήματα … θέσαν is ‘laid woes on’. κακότητι is the house ‘baseness’, here in the dative, ‘through the baseness’, and γερόντων is ‘of the elders’; the next unit says what the elders did.

sentences.t:
οἵ μ’ ἐθέλοντα μάχεσθαι ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσιν
αὐτόν τ’ ἰσχανάασκον ἐρητύοντό τε λαόν·
sentences.tr:
hoi m’ ethelonta machesthai epi prymnēisi neessin
auton t’ ischanaaskon erētyonto te laon·
sentences.l:
who, me wishing to fight at the sterns of the ships,
kept holding me myself back and restraining the people;
sentences.i: who, when I wished to fight at the sterns of the ships, kept holding me back, me myself, and restraining the people as well;
sentences.n: οἵ ‘who’ are the elders. μ’ ἐθέλοντα μάχεσθαι is ‘me wishing to fight’, and ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσιν ‘at the sterns of the ships’. ἰσχανάασκον is the imperfect of ἰσχανάω ‘hold back’ with the suffix -σκ-, which makes it repeated action, ‘kept holding back’. ἐρητύοντο is the imperfect middle of ἐρητύω ‘restrain’. αὐτόν τ’ … λαόν τε is ‘both me myself … and the people’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δή ῥα τότε βλάπτε φρένας εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἡμετέρας, νῦν αὐτὸς ἐποτρύνει καὶ ἀνώγει.
sentences.tr:
all’ ei dē rha tote blapte phrenas euryopa Zeus
hēmeteras, nyn autos epotrynei kai anōgei.
sentences.l:
But if indeed then far-thundering Zeus was damaging
our wits, now he himself urges us on and bids.”
sentences.i: But if Zeus who thunders from afar was indeed damaging our wits at that time, now he himself urges us on and bids.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ εἰ δή ῥα τότε is ‘but if indeed then’, the time of the holding back. βλάπτε is the imperfect of βλάπτω ‘damage, disable’, with no augment, and φρένας ἡμετέρας is ‘our wits’. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is the stock phrase, ‘far-thundering’ in the literal layer and ‘who thunders from afar’ in the other, with the meaning of εὐρύοπα doubtful. ἐποτρύνει ‘urges on’; ἀνώγει is from ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense, ‘bids’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα μᾶλλον ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισιν ὄρουσαν.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara mallon ep’ Argeioisin orousan.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all the more sprang upon the Argives.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they sprang at the Argives all the more.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’, ἔφαθ’ being ἔφατο elided (the rough breathing of the next word turns τ to θ). οἳ δ’ ἄρα ‘and they then’ are the Trojans. μᾶλλον ‘more’, and ὄρουσαν is the aorist of ὀρούω ‘spring, rush’, with ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισιν ‘upon the Argives’.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ οὐκέτ’ ἔμιμνε·
sentences.tr: Aias d’ ouket’ emimne·
sentences.l: But Ajax no longer stayed;
sentences.i: But Ajax no longer stood his ground;
sentences.n: ἔμιμνε is the imperfect of μίμνω ‘stay, stand one’s ground’, here with the augment (contrast μίμνεν at 689). The raised stop closes the clause, and the next gives the reason.

sentences.t: βιάζετο γὰρ βελέεσσιν·
sentences.tr: biazeto gar beleessin·
sentences.l: for he was being forced by the missiles;
sentences.i: for the missiles were pressing him hard;
sentences.n: βιάζετο is the imperfect passive of βιάζομαι ‘be forced, be hard pressed’. βελέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of βέλος ‘missile’, the means. γάρ gives the reason for what the line before said.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀνεχάζετο τυτθόν, ὀϊόμενος θανέεσθαι
θρῆνυν ἐφ’ ἑπταπόδην, λίπε δ’ ἴκρια νηὸς ἐΐσης.
sentences.tr:
all’ anechazeto tytthon, oïomenos thaneesthai
thrēnyn eph’ heptapodēn, lipe d’ ikria nēos eïsēs.
sentences.l:
but he drew back a little, thinking that he would die,
onto a seven-foot footstool, and left the decking of the well-balanced ship.
sentences.i: but he drew back a little, thinking that he would die, to the seven-foot footstool, and left the decking of the well-balanced ship.
sentences.n: ἀνεχάζετο is the imperfect of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, and τυτθόν ‘a little’ is an adverb. ὀϊόμενος θανέεσθαι is ‘thinking he would die’: ὀΐομαι ‘suppose, expect’, and θανέεσθαι the uncontracted future infinitive of θνῄσκω. θρῆνυν ἐφ’ ἑπταπόδην is ‘onto the seven-foot footstool’, with ἐπί standing between the noun and its adjective. θρῆνυς is ordinarily a footstool; on a ship it is some raised part, and the exact fitting is not known. ἑπταπόδην is ἑπτά ‘seven’ and πούς ‘foot’. λίπε is an aorist with no augment, ‘left’. ἴκρια νηὸς ἐΐσης is ‘the decking of the well-balanced ship’, ἐΐσης being the house word, whose sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἑστήκει δεδοκημένος, ἔγχεϊ δ’ αἰεὶ
Τρῶας ἄμυνε νεῶν, ὅς τις φέροι ἀκάματον πῦρ·
sentences.tr:
enth’ ar’ ho g’ hestēkei dedokēmenos, encheï d’ aiei
Trōas amyne neōn, hos tis pheroi akamaton pyr·
sentences.l:
There he stood, on the watch, and with his spear ever
warded the Trojans from the ships, whoever might bring untiring fire;
sentences.i: There he stood on the watch, and with his spear he kept warding the Trojans off from the ships, whoever came carrying untiring fire;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ is ‘there, then, he’. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, used as ‘was standing’. δεδοκημένος is a perfect participle meaning ‘on the watch, waiting for’. ἄμυνε is the imperfect of ἀμύνω, here with the accusative of the men and the genitive of what they are kept from: ‘kept the Trojans from the ships’. ὅς τις φέροι is an optative of repeated action, ‘whoever might bring’, i.e. ‘any who came bringing’. ἀκάματον πῦρ is the house ‘untiring fire’.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δὲ σμερδνὸν βοόων Δαναοῖσι κέλευε·
sentences.tr: aiei de smerdnon booōn Danaoisi keleue·
sentences.l: and ever terribly shouting he bade the Danaans:
sentences.i: And ever shouting terribly he bade the Danaans:
sentences.n: This line is the same as 687; the English is the same. Here the raised stop is English’s colon, and Ajax’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.tr:
ō philoi hērōes Danaoi therapontes Arēos
aneres este philoi, mnēsasthe de thouridos alkēs.
sentences.l:
“O friends, heroes, Danaans, attendants of Ares,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might.
sentences.i: “Friends, Danaan heroes, attendants of Ares: be men, friends, and remember impetuous might.
sentences.n: Ajax speaks. The first line is the same as 2.110, and the second line also stands at 6.112, in Hector’s mouth. Δαναοί ‘Danaans’ is the army’s second name, and θεράποντες Ἄρηος ‘attendants of Ares’ is the stock phrase, translated every time. ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι is ‘be men, friends’, as at 661. μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative of μιμνῄσκομαι ‘remember, be mindful of’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς, the stock ‘impetuous might’.

sentences.t:
ἠέ τινάς φαμεν εἶναι ἀοσσητῆρας ὀπίσσω,
ἦέ τι τεῖχος ἄρειον, ὅ κ’ ἀνδράσι λοιγὸν ἀμύναι;
sentences.tr:
ēe tinas phamen einai aossētēras opissō,
ēe ti teichos areion, ho k’ andrasi loigon amynai;
sentences.l:
Or do we say that there are some helpers behind us,
or some stronger wall, which might ward ruin from men?
sentences.i: Do we think that there are helpers behind us, or some stronger wall that could ward ruin off from men?
sentences.n: This is one double question: ἠέ opens it and ἦέ gives the other choice. ἀοσσητῆρας ‘helpers’, ὀπίσσω ‘behind’. τεῖχος ἄρειον is ‘a stronger wall’, ἄρειον being a comparative of ἀγαθός in the sense ‘better, stronger’. ὅ κ’ … ἀμύναι is an optative with κε, ‘that could ward off’, with λοιγόν ‘ruin’ as object and ἀνδράσι ‘for men’, a dative of interest.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τι σχεδόν ἐστι πόλις πύργοις ἀραρυῖα,
ᾗ κ’ ἀπαμυναίμεσθ’ ἑτεραλκέα δῆμον ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
ou men ti schedon esti polis pyrgois araruia,
hēi k’ apamynaimesth’ heteralkea dēmon echontes·
sentences.l:
No city is at all near, fitted with towers,
where we might ward it off from ourselves, having a people other-strengthening;
sentences.i: There is no city near at hand, furnished with towers, where we could ward the danger off from ourselves with a people who would tip the balance;
sentences.n: οὐ μέν τι is ‘not indeed at all’, and σχεδόν ‘near’. πύργοις ἀραρυῖα is ‘fitted with towers’: ἀραρυῖα is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit, furnish’. ᾗ κ’ ἀπαμυναίμεσθ’ is a potential optative middle of ἀπαμύνω, ‘ward off from ourselves’, with no object given (the danger is understood), and ᾗ ‘where’. ἑτεραλκέα is built on ἕτερος ‘the other’ and ἀλκή ‘might’, ‘giving strength to the other side’; its sense is disputed. The literal layer keeps its parts, and the other says ‘tip the balance’, the house reading of this word. δῆμον is ‘a people’ here, not a place.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐν γὰρ Τρώων πεδίῳ πύκα θωρηκτάων
πόντῳ κεκλιμένοι ἑκὰς ἥμεθα πατρίδος αἴης·
sentences.tr:
all’ en gar Trōōn pediōi pyka thōrēktaōn
pontōi keklimenoi hekas hēmetha patridos aiēs·
sentences.l:
But we sit in the plain of the closely corseleted
Trojans, leaning on the sea, far from our fatherland;
sentences.i: But we are sitting in the plain of the closely corseleted Trojans, with our backs to the sea, far from our fatherland;
sentences.n: ἀλλά … γάρ is ‘but in fact’. ἐν … πεδίῳ is ‘in the plain’ with Τρώων πύκα θωρηκτάων ‘of the closely corseleted Trojans’ set between, the stock phrase from 689. κεκλιμένοι is the perfect passive participle of κλίνω ‘lean’, with πόντῳ in the dative: ‘leaning on the sea’. ἑκάς ‘far’ takes the genitive πατρίδος αἴης, ‘from the fatherland’, αἶα being epic for γαῖα. ἥμεθα is the first plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’.

sentences.t: τὼ ἐν χερσὶ φόως, οὐ μειλιχίῃ πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr: tō en chersi phoōs, ou meilichiēi polemoio.
sentences.l: so in the hands is the light, not in the gentleness of war.”
sentences.i: So our deliverance lies in our hands, not in any gentleness of war.”
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ, ‘therefore’, and ἐν χερσί ‘in the hands’ has no verb; ‘is’ is understood. φόως (= φάος) is literally ‘light’, which can stand for deliverance, as the English says; the literal layer keeps ‘light’. μειλιχίῃ is an abstract noun from μειλίχιος ‘gentle’, ‘gentleness’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ, καὶ μαιμώων ἔφεπ’ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι.
sentences.tr: ē, kai maimōōn ephep’ encheï oxyoenti.
sentences.l: He spoke, and raging he went after them with his sharp spear.
sentences.i: So he said, and went raging after them with his sharp spear.
sentences.n: ἦ here is ‘he said’, not the particle, and καί ‘and’. μαιμώων is the present participle of μαιμάω ‘rage’, the house ‘raging’, uncontracted. ἔφεπ’ is ἔφεπε, the imperfect of ἐφέπω ‘go after, ply’; it has no object, and the next sentence says whom he went for. ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι is the stock ‘sharp spear’.

sentences.t:
ὅς τις δὲ Τρώων κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ φέροιτο
σὺν πυρὶ κηλείῳ, χάριν Ἕκτορος ὀτρύναντος,
τὸν δ’ Αἴας οὔτασκε δεδεγμένος ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ·
sentences.tr:
hos tis de Trōōn koilēis epi nēusi pheroito
syn pyri kēleiōi, charin Hektoros otrynantos,
ton d’ Aias outaske dedegmenos encheï makrōi·
sentences.i: And any Trojan who came rushing at the hollow ships with blazing fire, to please Hector, who had urged them on, Ajax would stab as he waited for him with his long spear;
sentences.n: This is repeated action in the past: ὅς τις … φέροιτο is an optative, ‘whoever came bearing’, and the main verb οὔτασκε is the imperfect of οὐτάω ‘wound’ with the repeating suffix -σκ-: ‘would wound’ in the literal layer, ‘would stab’ in the other. φέροιτο is middle, ‘rush, bear himself on’. κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσί has the rare epic dative plural κοίλῃς (= κοίλαις), ‘against the hollow ships’. πυρὶ κηλείῳ is the house ‘blazing fire’; the sense of κηλέος is not certain. χάριν Ἕκτορος ὀτρύναντος is ‘as a favour to Hector, he having urged them’; Hector called for fire at 718. δεδεγμένος is the perfect participle of δέχομαι, ‘waiting for’, and ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is ‘with his long spear’.

sentences.t: δώδεκα δὲ προπάροιθε νεῶν αὐτοσχεδὸν οὖτα.
sentences.tr: dōdeka de proparoithe neōn autoschedon outa.
sentences.l: and twelve in front of the ships at close quarters he wounded.
sentences.i: and twelve he stabbed in front of the ships, at close quarters.
sentences.n: δώδεκα ‘twelve’ is the object of οὖτα, the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’; the verb means a thrust with a point and is not always fatal, the literal layer keeps ‘wounded’ and the other says ‘stabbed’. προπάροιθε νεῶν is ‘in front of the ships’, and αὐτοσχεδόν ‘at close quarters’ is the word of 708.
